category_title: High-intelligence elementary student with inattentive ADHD and executive functioning deficits
minimal_context: Gail and the school psychologist are working one-on-one during lunch recess to organize her desk and review her homework assignments.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Since we are here during lunch recess, let's pull everything out to organize your desk and check your missing homework assignments.

STUDENT: I'm glad you came to help me with this project. There are a lot of loose papers in here.

TUTOR: Let's look at these missing assignments. What is happening with your studying?

STUDENT: I don’t get good grades because I don’t study outside class.

TUTOR: You need to complete these assignments and turn them in on time.

STUDENT: I have too many things to do after school so I don’t always get my homework done. I just tell my mom, 'Later, mom, later. I’ll do it later.'

options.A: Implement organization techniques like a two-pocket folder for daily assignments, a homework journal signed by the teacher and parent, and holders to keep supplies contained within her desk.
options.B: Provide her with access to similar, but more socially appropriate, sensory stimulation during the session, such as giving her a squishy stress-relief ball.
options.C: Model caring and cooperation, show positive regard, and actively redirect any anti-social behaviors during the one-on-one sessions.
options.D: Compromise, negotiate situations, and share decisions and power with the student regarding her assignments instead of imposing control.
